title: Ford Hypercar Completes Its First On-Track Test

body_markdown:
It is only appropriate that Ford’s new Hypercar performed its first real-world track test in France. Though proximity to the headquarters of chassis partner Oreca is surely the real reason, fans of endurance racing know where we’re going with this: The[24 Hours of Le Mans](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/24-hours-of-le-mans/) , the crown jewel of the endurance racing calendar, held on a mix of public roads and dedicated race track, is in France. Ford wants to win Le Mans—not just the GT class the Mustangs run in, but the whole thing.


That’s why,[nearly 19 months ago](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/ford-targets-overall-win-at-le-mans-in-2027-will-use-imsa-to-prepare/) , Ford announced it would enter the top class of Le Mans. The car you see here is the fruit of that labor, a “prototype” race car built from scratch for the top class of Le Mans, known as Hypercar. (This is the top class for the World Endurance Championship, or WEC, one of the sanctioning bodies of the 24 Hours of Le Mans.) That prototype has just completed a 1000-kilometer (621-mile), three-day test on the Paul Ricard Circuit in southern France. That’s a huge milestone, because the car needs to be ready in the first quarter of 2027.


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography


Dan Sayers, L, and Mark Rushbrook, R.


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography


“Reaching Paul Ricard and getting the car through its shakedown and three full days of running is exactly the milestone we set out to hit,” says Dan Sayers,[who left Red Bull Powertrains to manage Ford’s WEC Hypercar program](https://www.hagerty.com/media/motorsports/ford-plans-to-build-its-new-hypercar-racer-mostly-in-house/) . “Everything we did in the buildup—the dyno work in Dearborn, the[fire-up in France](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/hear-fords-le-mans-hypercar-crank-to-life/) , the countless hours in the sim—was about making sure that when we rolled out onto track, we were ready to be plug-and-play. There’s a long list of milestones still ahead of us before Q1 2027, but these past couple of weeks \[have\] given the team a lot of confidence and strong foundations to build on.”


Matt Campbell


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography


An important part of any race-car shakedown, of course, is the driver. For the World Endurance Championship in which Ford’s Hypercar will compete, each car has three drivers (though for the shorter races, each car may only run with two drivers). All six were present at Paul Ricard during testing week: the American Logan Sargeant, Australian Matt Campbell, British-born Swede Tom Blomqvist, and Germany’s Mike Rockenfeller all took turns in the cockpit. Sebastian Priaulx and Nick Yelloly were onsite “gathering feedback.”


Campbell, who currently drives a prototype for Porsche in IMSA, was present during the whole test and got the most track time in the Ford Racing Hypercar. “I’m genuinely excited for what’s ahead with this car,” he says. “We know there’s a long road in front of us, but this has been a really positive start. \[…\] Aside from a few minor teething issues—which you’d expect at the beginning of a new program—everything has gone well.”


Campbell will fly to the U.S. for three days of sim work before flying back to Europe for the next test, at Portimão in Portugal. That, along with Sayers’ and Sargeant’s comments, highlights the importance of simulator work in developing today’s (and tomorrow’s) race cars.


“There have already been countless hours poured into this project, including a ton of time in the simulator, so we’ve had a massive head start,” says Sargeant. “Now it’s about making sure everything comes together flawlessly, and that’s the next step for us. We can honestly say we’ve started in the best possible way.”


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson P


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography


After its time at Paul Ricard, the Ford Racing Hypercar will test at Silverstone in England, at Monza and Imola in Italy, and at Aragon in Spain before heading stateside to test at the Circuit of the Americas (COTA) in Texas and at Sebring in Florida. (Imola is on the[2027 WEC calendar](https://www.fiawec.com/en/news/fia-wec-reveals-nine-round-2027-calendar-as-series-expands/13598) , as are Silverstone and COTA. Sebring is on the calendar for the WEC’s North American-based counterpart, the IMSA WeatherTech SportsCar Championship.)


Fans of all ages know how important this race is to Ford. The automaker[famously went 1-2-3 in 1966](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/entire-podium-of-1966-le-mans-gt40s-now-reunited-in-one-collection/) , breaking Ferrari’s five-year win streak. Ford then proceeded to capture the overall win in ’67, ’68, and ’69. But history isn’t the only reason: For Ford, its global racing efforts[go hand-in-hand](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/fords-global-racing-ambitions-go-hand-in-hand-with-developing-markets/) with its interest in developing markets. The recent influx of manufacturers shows that Hypercar (and the parallel class in IMSA, GTP) is the place to be for an OEM seeking to put its name on the international endurance-racing stage. (After all, WEC doesn’t let a manufacturer compete in lower classes under its own name and with a factory team.) Ford will join the 2027 Le Mans Hypercar grid along with McLaren and Genesis, where they will face recent overall winners Toyota and Ferrari, plus Aston Martin, Peugeot, Cadillac, and BMW.


Here’s how Mark Rushbrook, global director of Ford Racing, sees the recent test: “Every mile we put on this car brings us closer to Le Mans, and closer to reclaiming our place at the top of endurance racing.”


Michele Scudiero / Drew Gibson Photography
